body:
The Sultanate after the Tughlaqs

By the beginning of the 15th century, the Delhi Sultanate had lost effective control over many territories that earlier Sultans had conquered.

The weakening of the Tughlaqs, conflicts among nobles, the growing independence of provincial governors and Timur's invasion of 1398 contributed to this transformation.

The final 2 dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate were the Sayyids (1414–1451) and the Lodis (1451–1526).

Sayyid Dynasty: 1414–1451

Khizr Khan: Founder of the Sayyid Dynasty

Khizr Khan (1414–1421) established the Sayyid Dynasty after gaining control of Delhi in 1414.

He had earlier governed important northwestern territories, including Multan, and was associated with Timur's political authority.

Khizr Khan did not formally assume the title of Sultan. Instead, he acknowledged Timurid overlordship and used the title Rayat-i-Ala.

The dynasty's control was considerably smaller than that of the powerful Khalji and early Tughlaq rulers. Delhi's authority was largely concentrated in the northern plains, while important regions such as Gujarat and Bengal had separate rulers.

Other important Sayyid rulers

The main Sayyid rulers were:

  • Khizr Khan (1414–1421): Founder of the dynasty.
  • Mubarak Shah (1421–1434): Attempted to strengthen royal authority and suppress opposition.
  • Muhammad Shah: Ruled during continued political weakness and increasing pressure from regional powers.
  • Alauddin Alam Shah: The last Sayyid ruler, who withdrew from active control of Delhi.

By 1451, the Sayyid Dynasty had lost the ability to retain the throne. Bahlul Lodi assumed power and founded the next dynasty.

Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid Dynasty in 1414. He should not be confused with Khizr Khan, the son of Alauddin Khalji, who belonged to the earlier Khalji period.

Lodi Dynasty: 1451–1526

The Lodi Dynasty was the fifth and final ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.

The Lodis were of Afghan origin. This distinguished them from the predominantly Turkish political background of the earlier Mamluk rulers.

Bahlul Lodi: Founder and territorial consolidation

Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) established the dynasty in 1451.

He strengthened the political position of the Afghan nobility and attempted to recover territories that had become independent during the declining Tughlaq and Sayyid periods.

His most important territorial achievement was the recovery of Jaunpur, where the Sharqi rulers had established an independent kingdom. Bahlul defeated the Sharqi power and brought Jaunpur back under the authority of Delhi.

His success strengthened Lodi rule in the northern Gangetic plains.

Sikandar Lodi: Agra and administrative consolidation

Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) succeeded Bahlul Lodi.

He strengthened royal authority, extended control in northern India and developed Agra as an important political and military centre.

Agra was established as a major Lodi administrative centre around 1504–1505. The settlement existed earlier, so Sikandar's achievement is more precisely described as its development or re-establishment as a major capital city.

Sikandar Lodi is also associated with a standard land-measurement unit known as the Gaz-i-Sikandari or Sikandari gaz.

These measures supported more organised administration and revenue assessment.

Ibrahim Lodi: The last Sultan of Delhi

Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) was the last ruler of the Lodi Dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate.

He attempted to strengthen the authority of the Sultan over powerful Afghan nobles. His relations with several nobles deteriorated, causing political instability and opposition to his rule.

Some dissatisfied nobles, including Daulat Khan Lodi of Punjab, sought assistance from Babur, the Timurid ruler based in Kabul.

The First Battle of Panipat, 1526

The decisive battle between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi occurred at Panipat on 21 April 1526.

Babur's army defeated Ibrahim Lodi, who was killed in the battle.

Babur's victory was aided by effective battlefield organisation, cavalry tactics and the use of artillery. Internal divisions among the Afghan nobility also weakened Ibrahim Lodi's political position.

The battle had 2 major consequences:

  • It ended the Lodi Dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate.
  • It marked the beginning of Mughal rule in northern India.

First Battle of Panipat: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526. Ibrahim Lodi was the last Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate, while Babur founded Mughal rule.

Gujarat during the decline of the Delhi Sultanate

Gujarat provides an important example of the change from central Sultanate authority to regional independence.

Alauddin Khalji conquered Gujarat in 1299, bringing the region under the political authority of Delhi. Anhilwara or Patan was an important centre involved in this conquest.

As the Tughlaq Dynasty weakened, provincial governors in different parts of India acquired greater independence. Gujarat developed into a separate regional kingdom.

Zafar Khan, who had governed Gujarat, assumed the title Muzaffar Shah I in 1407. This marked the formal establishment of independent Sultanate rule in Gujarat.

The Gujarat Sultanate subsequently developed as an important regional power. Ahmad Shah I established Ahmedabad in 1411, creating a major new political centre.

The important chronological distinction is that Gujarat came under Delhi during Khalji expansion but developed independent rule during the decline of Tughlaq authority.

The Gujarat Sultanate was a separate regional kingdom. It was not a sixth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.

Understanding the political transition

The history of the Delhi Sultanate can be understood as a sequence of changes in political authority.

The Mamluks established and consolidated the Sultanate. The Khaljis expanded its territorial and military reach. The Tughlaqs initially extended this reach further, but the state subsequently weakened through rebellions, administrative difficulties and territorial losses.

The Sayyids governed a much reduced kingdom. The Lodis restored some northern territories but ultimately lost Delhi to Babur in 1526.

This sequence explains why the Sultanate's political history involves both expansion and fragmentation rather than uninterrupted territorial growth.

Prelims focus

  • 1414: Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid Dynasty.
  • 1451: Bahlul Lodi founded the Lodi Dynasty, the first Afghan dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Bahlul Lodi: Recovered Jaunpur from the Sharqi rulers.
  • Sikandar Lodi: Developed Agra as a major political centre around 1504–1505.
  • 1407: Zafar Khan assumed the title Muzaffar Shah I in Gujarat.
  • 1526: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat.
  • Trap: The independent Gujarat Sultanate was not one of the 5 ruling dynasties of Delhi.

E. pictures.alt: Tughlaq decline left Delhi under Sayyid and Lodi rule alongside independent regional kingdoms; Gujarat stayed separate, while Bahlul Lodi recovered Jaunpur.
pictures.caption: The decline of Tughlaq authority allowed regional kingdoms to emerge before the Sayyid and Lodi periods.

pictures.alt: A succession diagram links the 5 Delhi Sultanate dynasties to their founders, founding years and key rulers, ending with Ibrahim Lodi’s defeat in 1526.
pictures.caption: The 5 Delhi Sultanate dynasties and the rulers most closely associated with their major political developments.

title: Sayyid and Lodi Dynasties (1414–1526): Regional Kingdoms and the End of the Sultanate
